standard_text: Apply the properties of operations (e.g., identity, inverse, commutative, associative, distributive properties) to create equivalent linear expressions, including situations that involve factoring out a common number (e.g., given 2x - 10, create an equivalent expression 2(x - 5)). Justify each step in the process.

progression.narrative:
This standard is about rewriting a linear expression as an equal-value expression that LOOKS different, and being able to name the property that makes each move legal. The verbs do the organizing: apply the properties, create an equivalent expression, factor out a common number, and justify each step. So the progression starts where the properties first bite: collecting like terms. Adding or subtracting two linear expressions is really the commutative and associative properties letting you regroup x-terms with x-terms and numbers with numbers -- and the whole thing lives or dies on carrying every sign, because there is no calculator on this standard. Once a student can combine like terms, the standard's own demand to 'justify each step' gets its own skill: looking at a single move and naming whether it was commutative, associative, distributive, or identity.

From there the two engines the standard names take over. Distribution -- a rational number outside the parentheses multiplying every term inside -- is the expansion move, and its hard cases are negative and fractional coefficients where a sign or a skipped term wrecks the result. Factoring is the same property run backwards: pull out the greatest common number so the expression reads p(qx + r), exactly the form the content limits require and the shape of the standard's own 2x - 10 = 2(x - 5) example. With expand and factor both in hand, the At-proficiency core is putting them together -- simplify a multi-part expression that needs distributing AND combining, justifying each step -- which is also where the most expensive errors hide, because one early sign slip corrupts everything after it. Finally, the Above-proficiency payoff turns outward: create MULTIPLE equivalent forms of one expression and prove they are equal, which is where substitution becomes the tool that certifies equivalence. The order is deliberate: combine, then name the property, then distribute, then factor, then combine operations, then generate and verify multiple forms. Underneath all of it runs one habit -- an equivalent expression is one that gives the same value for every input, and every legal step can be named by a property.

steps.rationale: The lowest-band engine task is finding a missing coefficient by adding two linear expressions. Collecting like terms -- x-terms together, constants together, every sign carried -- is the commutative/associative property in action and the first way the standard creates an equivalent expression.

The standard explicitly says 'justify each step.' Before a student can justify their own work, they must be able to look at a single equivalence step and name the property (commutative, associative, distributive, identity) that makes it legal.

The At-proficiency core: apply the distributive property to expand a rational coefficient over a parenthesis and then combine like terms. The hard cases -- negative and fractional coefficients -- are the real difficulty and must be reliable before they can be one step inside a bigger problem.

The standard names factoring out a common number explicitly, with its own worked example (2x - 10 = 2(x - 5)). Factoring is distribution reversed: pull the greatest common factor to write p(qx + r), the exact form the content limits require.

The full At-proficiency demand: simplify a multi-part expression using several operations at once (distribute, subtract a group, combine) and justify each step -- and, by extension, find the first error in someone else's multi-step work. This is where an early sign slip corrupts the whole result.

The Above-proficiency payoff: generate MULTIPLE equivalent expressions from one, and prove equivalence. Substitution becomes the certifying tool -- two forms are equivalent only if they give the same value for every input.

skills.name: Add, subtract, and multiply signed rational numbers

prerequisite_skill.description: Add, subtract, and multiply positive and negative integers and simple rational numbers without a calculator.

skills.i_do_script: Before we touch any variables, we have to be fast and correct with signed numbers, because there is NO calculator on this standard -- but fast comes AFTER the rules make sense. Watch the pattern: 3 x (-3) = -9, 2 x (-3) = -6, 1 x (-3) = -3, 0 x (-3) = 0. Each step climbs by 3, so past zero the pattern forces (-1) x (-3) = +3 ... all the way to (-5) x (-3) = +15. A negative times a negative is POSITIVE because the pattern demands it. Subtracting a negative works the same way: 5 - 2 = 3, 5 - 1 = 4, 5 - 0 = 5 -- so 5 - (-1) must be 6. Subtracting a negative adds. Now the rules I run at speed: a negative times a positive is negative (-4 x 3 = -12); both negative when adding means add and keep the sign (-7 + (-5) = -12); negative times negative is positive; subtracting a negative flips to adding (-3 - (-7) becomes -3 + 7 = 4).

canonical_error.pattern: Mishandles a sign -- makes a negative times a negative come out negative, or treats subtracting a negative as subtracting a positive
canonical_error.example: Computes -6 times -2 as -12 instead of +12, or -3 - (-7) as -10 instead of +4
canonical_error.why: The student applies the visible minus sign to the answer instead of following the signed-number rules. Negative times negative is positive, and subtracting a negative reverses to addition -- these are the exact operations distributing and combining will demand on every problem.

skills.item_template: A single signed-number computation (add, subtract, or multiply) with integers or simple rationals. Short numeric response; good rapid fluency bank.

redirect_script.stop: Wait -- what are the two signs doing here?
redirect_script.prompt: Run the pattern past zero: 3 x (-3), 2 x (-3), 1 x (-3), 0 x (-3) -- what does the climb force next? Name the two signs first, then apply the rule out loud: negative times negative is positive; subtracting a negative flips to adding. Write the sign of the answer BEFORE the digits.
redirect_script.praise: You applied the sign rule before computing -- that's the fluency this standard needs.

vocabulary.definition: Any number that can be written as a fraction of two integers, including integers, fractions, and decimals.
A whole number or its opposite, like -3, 0, or 7.

worked_example_script.text: Write the pattern column: 3 x (-3) = -9, 2 x (-3) = -6, 1 x (-3) = -3, 0 x (-3) = 0.
Each answer climbs by 3. Keep the pattern going: (-1) x (-3) = ? ... all the way down to (-5) x (-3) = ?
The pattern forces (-5) x (-3) = +15 -- negative times negative is positive because the climb doesn't stop at zero.
Same move for subtraction: 5 - 2 = 3, 5 - 1 = 4, 5 - 0 = 5 ... so what must 5 - (-1) be? What is subtracting a negative really doing?
Write '-5 times -3' and '-8 - (-2).'
For the first one, what are the two signs? What does negative times negative give?
Negative times negative is positive, so -5 times -3 = +15. For -8 - (-2), subtracting a negative flips to adding: -8 + 2 = -6.
If the student writes -15 or -10, stop and ask 'what is the rule for these two signs?'
Your turn: -9 times -1, and -4 - (-9).

skills.name: Identify terms, coefficients, and like terms in an expression

prerequisite_skill.description: Name the parts of an algebraic term -- coefficient, variable, and constant -- and tell which terms are alike.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: In 5x + 3, what is the coefficient of x, and is 3 a like term with 5x?

skills.i_do_script: Picture x as a sealed bag holding a number nobody knows, so 7x is 7 bags and a plain number like 4 is loose counters -- bags and loose counters are different kinds of things, and only pieces of the same kind can ever pile together. Every expression is built from terms -- the pieces separated by + or - signs. In 5x + 3 there are two terms: 5x and 3. The 5 is the coefficient (the number multiplying x) and 3 is a constant (a plain number). Like terms have the exact same variable part, so 4x and 2x are like terms, but 4x and 7 are NOT -- a term with an x and a plain number can never be combined. Naming these parts is what lets us decide, later, which pieces are allowed to merge.

canonical_error.pattern: Treats a constant as a like term with a variable term, or reads the sign in front of a term as belonging to the wrong term
canonical_error.example: Calls 4x and 7 like terms in 4x + 7 - 2x, or reads the -2x as +2x because it ignores the minus in front
canonical_error.why: The student groups by 'they are all numbers' instead of by identical variable part, and detaches the leading sign from its term. A term's sign lives directly in front of it, and only terms with the identical variable part are alike.

skills.item_template: An expression; student names a coefficient, counts terms, identifies the constant, or picks the like terms. Short response fluency bank.

sample_items.stem: In 5x + 3, what is the coefficient of x?
How many terms are in 3x - 8 + x?
What is the constant term in 6x - 2?

sample_items.answer: No -- one has a variable and one is a plain number.

redirect_script.stop: Do those two terms have the SAME variable part?
redirect_script.prompt: Ask the table question first: is that piece a bag (an x) or a loose counter (a plain number)? Underline the variable part of each term. Only terms with the identical variable part are alike; a plain number is never like an x-term. And read the sign directly in front of each term as part of it.
redirect_script.praise: You grouped by the variable part and kept each sign with its term -- that's how terms work.

vocabulary.definition: A single number or variable piece separated by + or -, like the 5x and the 3 in 5x + 3.
The rational number multiplied by a variable, like the 5 in 5x or the 1/2 in (1/2)x.
A plain number with no variable, like the 3 in 5x + 3.

worked_example_script.text: Before we name anything, picture 7x - 4 + 2x as stuff on a table: 7 bags of x, then 4 counters taken away, then 2 more bags of x. Which pieces are the same kind of thing, and which piece has no bag at all?
Write '7x - 4 + 2x.'
How many terms are there? Which have an x, and which is a plain number?
Three terms: 7x, -4, and 2x. The x-terms are 7x and 2x -- those are like terms. The -4 is a constant and stands alone.
If the student says -4 is a like term with the x's, ask 'does -4 have an x?'
Your turn: in 3x + 6 - x, name the like terms and the constant.

skills.name: Combine like terms to create an equivalent linear expression
skills.i_do_script: Think of -y as one bag of y you OWE, not one you own -- an owed bag cancels one of your real bags. Put the piles on the table first and the count comes out on its own. To create an equivalent expression by adding or subtracting, I combine like terms: x-terms with x-terms, numbers with numbers, and I keep every sign. Watch: (-y + 5) + (7y - 9). The y-terms are -1y and 7y; -1 + 7 = 6, so 6y. The numbers are 5 and -9; 5 - 9 = -4. So the equivalent expression is 6y - 4. The number stuck to the first y is -1, not 1 -- dropping that negative is the classic mistake.

canonical_error.pattern: Drops the negative on a variable term (or combines a variable term with a constant) when collecting like terms
canonical_error.example: For (-y + 5) + (7y - 9) the student treats -y as +y, computing 1 + 7 = 8 and reporting 8y instead of 6y
canonical_error.why: The student reads the coefficient of -y as 1 rather than -1, so the sign is lost before the terms are added. Every term carries the sign directly in front of it, and that sign must travel with the coefficient when like terms are combined.

skills.item_template: Two linear binomials added, with one coefficient unknown (n*var + b), or a two-expression sum to simplify. Integer or simple rational coefficients; one variable. Short numeric/expression response.

sample_items.stem: Enter the value of n so that (-y + 5) + (7y - 9) is equivalent to (ny - 4).
sample_items.distractor_logic: -1 + 7 = 6. Reading -y as +y gives the trap answer 8; combining the constants into the coefficient gives other wrong values.
2 + 5 = 7 and 6 - 1 = 5. Adding 6 + 1 or 2 + 5 + 6 - 1 into one number are the common slips.
3 + (-6) = -3 and 2 + 3 = 5. Reading -6x as +6x gives 9x, the sign-drop error.

sample_items.stem: Enter the value of n so that (4x - 7) + (-9x + 2) is equivalent to (nx - 5).
sample_items.distractor_logic: 4 + (-9) = -5; the constants -7 + 2 = -5 confirm the form. Dropping the negative on -9x gives +13 or +5.

redirect_script.stop: Wait -- what sign is in front of that term?
redirect_script.prompt: Look back at the piles: is that first bag one you own or one you OWE? Write the sign directly on the coefficient: -y means -1y. Then add the variable terms in one pile and the numbers in another, carrying every sign.
redirect_script.praise: You carried the negative with the term -- that's how like terms really combine.

vocabulary.definition: Terms with the exact same variable part, so their coefficients can be added.
Two expressions that give the same value for every value of the variable.
The rational number multiplied by a variable, like the -1 in -y or the 7 in 7y.

worked_example_script.text: Sketch (-y + 5) + (7y - 9) as piles: 1 bag of y OWED and 5 counters, next to 7 bags of y and 9 counters OWED.
Push all the bags together: you hold 7 bags but owe 1 -- how many bags are really yours? Now the counters: you hold 5 but owe 9 -- where does that leave you?

The owed bag cancels one of the 7, leaving 6 bags; 5 counters against 9 owed leaves 4 owed. That is 6y - 4. Counting 8 bags means you counted the OWED bag as one you own -- the pile picture catches it instantly.
Which terms have a y? What is the sign in front of the first y?
The y-terms are -1y and 7y: -1 + 7 = 6, so 6y. The numbers are 5 and -9: 5 - 9 = -4. Result: 6y - 4.
If the student writes 8y, stop and ask 'is the first term +y or -y?'
Your turn: (3x + 2) + (-6x + 3).

practice_problems.stem: Enter the value of n so that (-y + 5) + (7y - 9) is equivalent to (ny - 4).
practice_problems.notes: Spec Below item; baits reading -y as +y.
Straight combine, positive coefficients.

practice_problems.stem: Riley combined the like terms in (-y + 5) + (7y - 9). Find and fix the mistake.
practice_problems.answer: Riley dropped the negative on the first y. It is -1y, so -1 + 7 = 6, not 8. The correct equivalent expression is 6y - 4.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: sign lost on a leading -y term.
Negative x-coefficient in the second group.

practice_problems.stem: Enter the value of n so that (4x - 7) + (-9x + 2) is equivalent to (nx - 5).
practice_problems.notes: Both coefficient and constant land on -5 -- must keep them separate.

practice_problems.stem: Write two binomials whose sum is 5x - 3, then check by combining.
practice_problems.notes: Reversed direction -- build a pair with a known sum.

activities.title: Like or Unlike
activities.instructions:
1. Each card shows two terms.
2. Decide if they are like terms (same variable part) or not.
3. Sort the card into 'Like terms' or 'Not like terms.'
4. Rule to place a card: if they are alike, write their combined value; if not, say why in one word.
5. Debrief: which pairs tricked people because one term hid a negative sign?

activities.title: The Vanishing Negative
materials: Slip with Riley's combine ending in 8y - 4
activities.instructions:
1. Read Riley's work on (-y + 5) + (7y - 9), which ends in 8y - 4.
2. Circle the exact spot where the negative on -y disappeared.
3. Redo the y-terms with the sign carried, and write the correct answer.
4. Write the one rule that prevents this error every time.

content.error_step: Riley read -y as if its coefficient were +1 instead of -1.
content.why: The coefficient of -y is -1, so -1 + 7 = 6. The correct equivalent expression is 6y - 4, not 8y - 4.

strategy_links.why: The dropped-sign error is precise and baitable, making find-and-fix the ideal routine for combining like terms.
Choral response on 'the sign in front of the term travels with it' hard-wires the habit that prevents sign drops.
Number-talk style mental combining ('what is -1 plus 7?') builds the signed-arithmetic fluency this skill rides on.

questioning_prompts: Which terms are alike here, and which stand alone?
What is the sign in front of that first term?
What do the x-terms combine to? What do the numbers combine to?
How could you check that your expression is equivalent to the original?
Did any negative sign go missing between the start and your answer?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student drops the negative on a leading -y term, or combines a variable term with a constant.
misconception_redirects.say: Write the sign directly on the coefficient: -y means -1y. Then add the x-terms in one pile and the numbers in another, carrying every sign.
misconception_redirects.praise: You carried the negative with the term -- that's how like terms really combine.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student merges an x-term with a constant (e.g., 3x + 5 becomes 8x).
misconception_redirects.say: An x-term and a plain number are not alike -- they stay separate. Keep the x-terms in one pile and the numbers in another.
misconception_redirects.praise: You kept the x-terms and the numbers apart -- that's what 'like terms' means.

quick_checks.look_for: 4x - 5. An answer of 6x or 4x + 5 signals a dropped sign on -x or on -9.

quick_checks.prompt: Find n so that (2x - 3) + (x + 3) is equivalent to nx.
quick_checks.look_for: n = 3 (constants cancel to 0). A leftover constant means the student did not combine -3 + 3.

sentence_starters: The x-terms are ___ and ___, which combine to ___.
I kept the sign in front of each term, so the equivalent expression is ___.

steps.annotation: Commutative and associative properties let me regroup y-terms and numbers.
The first term is -1y -- carry the negative.
Numbers combine with the numbers.
One y-term and one constant -- fully combined.
Put x-terms with x-terms, numbers with numbers.
Carry the negative on -6x.
Combine the constants 2 + 3.
Write the equivalent expression: one x-term, one number.

skills.name: Identify the property of operations that justifies a step
skills.i_do_script: Justifying a step means naming the property that makes it legal. The four we use: commutative (change the ORDER, like 3 + x = x + 3), associative (change the GROUPING, like (2 + x) + 5 = 2 + (x + 5)), distributive (a number outside parentheses multiplies each term inside, like 3(x + 2) = 3x + 6), and identity (adding 0 or multiplying by 1 changes nothing). Watch: 5(x + 3) = 5x + 15 -- the 5 reached both terms inside, so that is the distributive property, not commutative.

canonical_error.pattern: Confuses the distributive property with commutative/associative, or swaps commutative (order) and associative (grouping)
canonical_error.example: Labels 3(x + 2) = 3x + 6 as the commutative property because the terms look rearranged, when multiplying across the parentheses is the distributive property
canonical_error.why: The student matches by surface appearance instead of what actually changed. Distributive means a number multiplied every term inside parentheses; commutative means only the order changed; associative means only the grouping (parentheses) moved.

skills.item_template: A single equivalence step shown; student selects the property (commutative, associative, distributive, identity) that justifies it. Integer coefficients. Multiple choice.

sample_items.distractor_logic: A number multiplied each term inside the parentheses -- that is distribution. The rearranged look tempts 'commutative.'
Only the grouping (parentheses) moved; order and values stayed -- that is associative, not commutative.
Only the order of the two terms flipped -- commutative. No grouping changed and nothing was distributed.

sample_items.stem: Which property is demonstrated? x + 0 = x
sample_items.distractor_logic: Adding 0 leaves the value unchanged -- the additive identity. Inverse would be x + (-x) = 0.

redirect_script.stop: What actually changed from the left side to the right?
redirect_script.prompt: Ask one question: did a number get multiplied into a parenthesis (distributive), did only the ORDER flip (commutative), or did only the GROUPING move (associative)? Point to the exact change.
redirect_script.praise: You named the property by what changed, not by how it looks -- that's real justification.

vocabulary.definition: You can change the order of terms in addition or multiplication: a + b = b + a.
You can change the grouping (the parentheses) without changing the value: (a + b) + c = a + (b + c).
A number outside parentheses multiplies each term inside: a(b + c) = ab + ac.
Adding 0 or multiplying by 1 leaves a number unchanged: x + 0 = x.

worked_example_script.text: What did the 5 do to get to the right side?
The 5 multiplied each term inside the parentheses: 5 times x is 5x, 5 times 3 is 15. A number multiplying each term inside is the distributive property.
If the student says 'commutative,' ask 'did only the ORDER change, or did a number multiply into the parentheses?'
Your turn: name the property in (2 + x) + 5 = 2 + (x + 5).

practice_problems.stem: What does the distributive property let you do to a(b + c)?
practice_problems.answer: Multiply a by each term inside: ab + ac.

practice_problems.notes: Spec-style; baits 'commutative.'
Only grouping moved.

practice_problems.stem: Casey said the step 5(x + 3) = 5x + 15 shows the commutative property. Find and fix the mistake.
shown_work: Casey wrote: 'The terms got rearranged, so it is commutative.'
practice_problems.answer: Nothing was reordered -- the 5 multiplied each term inside the parentheses (5 times x, 5 times 3). That is the distributive property, not commutative.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: calling distribution 'commutative' by surface look.
Additive identity -- adding 0.

practice_problems.stem: Give your own example of the commutative property of multiplication using a variable.
practice_problems.answer: Sample: 3x = x times 3 (or 4 times x = x times 4).
practice_problems.notes: Reversed direction -- produce, not just recognize.

practice_problems.stem: Explain in one sentence the difference between the commutative and associative properties.
practice_problems.answer: Commutative changes the ORDER of terms; associative changes only the GROUPING (the parentheses).
practice_problems.notes: Forces articulating the distinction the distractors exploit.

activities.title: Sort by Property
activities.instructions:
1. Each card shows one equivalence step (like '4x + 7 = 7 + 4x').
2. Decide what actually changed: order, grouping, a distribution, or an identity move.
3. Sort the card under Commutative, Associative, Distributive, or Identity.
4. Rule to place a card: say in one sentence what changed.
5. Debrief: which cards looked commutative but were really distributive?

cards.text: (3 times 2) times x = 3 times (2 times x)

activities.title: Name That Property
materials: Card set: 5 step cards and 5 property-name cards (two look-alike decoys)
activities.instructions:
1. Match each equivalence step to the property that justifies it.
2. Two property names are decoys that DON'T match any step -- set them aside and say why.
3. To claim a match, name what changed from left to right.
4. Debrief: how do you tell commutative from associative in one look?

strategy_links.why: Think-pair-share on 'what actually changed?' surfaces the reasoning that distinguishes the four properties.
Mislabeling distribution as commutative is a precise, high-frequency error ideal for find-and-fix.
Choral response on 'order, grouping, or distribute?' builds the quick property-naming this skill needs.

questioning_prompts: What is different between the left side and the right side?
Did a number multiply into a parenthesis, or did only the order change?
Is this a change of ORDER or a change of GROUPING?
Could you write your own example of that property?
Which property would justify undoing this step?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student labels a distribution as commutative, or swaps commutative and associative.
misconception_redirects.say: Ask one question: did a number get multiplied into a parenthesis (distributive), did only the ORDER flip (commutative), or did only the GROUPING move (associative)? Point to the exact change.
misconception_redirects.praise: You named the property by what changed, not by how it looks -- that's real justification.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student calls x + 0 = x the inverse property.
misconception_redirects.say: Identity means adding 0 (or multiplying by 1) leaves the value alone. Inverse would be x + (-x) = 0 -- a number and its opposite.
misconception_redirects.praise: You separated identity from inverse -- adding 0 keeps the value, opposites make 0.

quick_checks.look_for: Distributive. 'Commutative' diagnoses matching by look instead of by what changed.
Associative. 'Commutative' means the student confused grouping with order.

sentence_starters: From left to right, the ___ changed, so this is the ___ property.
It is not ___ because ___ did not change.

steps.annotation: The 5 outside the parentheses is gone; it now multiplies each inside term.
A number multiplying every term inside is the pattern a(b + c) = ab + ac.
Nothing merely swapped places, so it is not commutative.
Multiplying across the parentheses is the distributive property.
Same terms in the same order -- 2, x, 5.
Only the grouping changed, not the order or the values.
Decide: is a change of grouping commutative or associative?
Name the property.

skills.name: Distribute a rational coefficient and combine like terms
skills.i_do_script: Before any rule, let a pattern set the signs: multiplying 3x - 7 by 2, then 1, then 0 steps the answer down by 3x and UP by 7 each time -- and nothing stops that ladder at zero. Distributing means the number outside the parentheses multiplies EVERY term inside, and the signs come along. Watch a tricky one: -4(3x - 7). The -4 hits 3x: -4 times 3 is -12, so -12x. The -4 hits -7: negative times negative is POSITIVE, so +28. The result is -12x + 28. After distributing I combine any like terms -- for 5x + (1/2)(4x - 8), I distribute to get 2x - 4, then 5x + 2x = 7x, giving 7x - 4.

canonical_error.pattern: Distributes to the first term only, or keeps the wrong sign on the second product (misses that negative times negative is positive)
canonical_error.example: For -4(3x - 7) the student writes -12x - 28, keeping the minus instead of computing -4 times -7 = +28
canonical_error.why: The student applies the outside number's sign to the operation instead of computing a signed product, or treats the parenthesis as attached only to the leading term. Both terms must be multiplied, and negative times negative is positive.

skills.item_template: An expression p(qx + r) with a rational p (negative or fractional), optionally added to a loose like term. Student distributes and combines. Integer, decimal, or fraction coefficients. Short response.

sample_items.stem: Use the distributive property to simplify: -4(3x - 7).
sample_items.distractor_logic: -4 times 3x = -12x; -4 times -7 = +28. '-12x - 28' keeps the minus (misses negative times negative).
(1/2)(4x - 8) = 2x - 4, then 5x + 2x = 7x. Forgetting to multiply the -8 by 1/2 leaves 5x + 2x - 8.
-0.8 times (10.8x + 3.2x = 14x) = -11.2x; -0.8 times -20 = +16. Missing the +16 sign or not combining the x-terms yields the distractors.
3 times 2x = 6x; 3 times 5 = 15. '6x + 5' skips the second product.

redirect_script.stop: Did the outside number reach the SECOND term too?
redirect_script.prompt: Check the ladder first: as the outside number steps below zero, which way is the constant moving? Draw an arrow from the outside number to each term inside and say the product out loud with its sign: 'negative four times negative seven is positive twenty-eight.' Then combine like terms.
redirect_script.praise: You multiplied both terms and kept the signs straight -- clean distribution.

vocabulary.definition: A number outside parentheses multiplies each term inside: a(b + c) = ab + ac.
A single number or variable piece separated by + or -, like the 3x and the -7 in 3x - 7.
The rational number multiplied by a variable, like the -4 in -4(3x - 7) or the 1/2 in (1/2)(4x - 8).

worked_example_script.text: Each step down, the x-part drops by 3x and the number CLIMBS by 7. Keep stepping below zero: -1(3x - 7) = ? Then -2, -3, all the way to -4(3x - 7) = ?
The ladder forces -3x + 7, then -6x + 14, -9x + 21, and -12x + 28. The constant keeps climbing into the positives, so -4(3x - 7) MUST end in +28 -- writing -28 breaks a pattern you can see.
How many terms are inside? So how many products will we get?
Two terms, two products. -4 times 3x is -12x. -4 times -7 is +28 -- negative times negative is positive. Result: -12x + 28.
If the student writes -12x - 28, ask 'what is negative times negative?'
Your turn: 5x + (1/2)(4x - 8). Distribute, then combine.

practice_problems.notes: Spec At item; negative times negative on the second term.
Spec At item; fractional coefficient plus a loose x-term.

practice_problems.stem: Morgan distributed -4(3x - 7). Find and fix the mistake.
practice_problems.answer: The second product is wrong: -4 times -7 is +28, not -28. Negative times negative is positive. The correct expression is -12x + 28.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: sign slip on the negative-times-negative product.
Spec At item; decimal coefficients, three inside terms.
Two distributions plus a subtracted group -- the structure of the multi-step skill ahead.

practice_problems.stem: Fill in the blank: -3(2x ___ ) = -6x + 9. What term is missing?
practice_problems.notes: Reversed direction -- recover the inside term from the expanded form.

activities.title: Expand and Match
materials: Card set: 6 p(qx + r) cards and 8 expanded-form cards (two sign-trap decoys)
activities.instructions:
1. Lay out the folded-form cards and the expanded-form cards.
2. Match each p(qx + r) to its correct expansion.
3. Two expanded cards are decoys with a flipped sign on the second term -- set them aside and name the error.
4. To claim a match, say both products out loud with their signs.
5. Debrief: which sign rule caught the most decoys?

activities.title: Sign Slip Hunt
materials: Slip with Morgan's distribution ending in -12x - 28
activities.instructions:
1. Read Morgan's expansion of -4(3x - 7) ending in -12x - 28.
2. Check each product separately: is -4 times -7 positive or negative?
3. Rewrite the correct expansion.
4. Write the one sign rule that fixes this error forever.

content.why: Negative times negative is positive: -4 times -7 = +28. The correct expansion is -12x + 28.

strategy_links.why: An area/box model for distribution makes 'every term inside gets multiplied' concrete before the abstract two-product rule.
The sign-slip and skip-the-second-term errors are precise and baitable -- ideal for find-and-fix.
Choral drill of signed products ('negative times negative is...') builds the automaticity distribution fluency requires.

questioning_prompts: How many terms are inside? How many products should you get?
What is the sign of the second product? Why?
Did the outside number reach the last term?
After distributing, are there any like terms left to combine?
How would you check your expansion with x = 1?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student distributes to the first term only or flips the sign on the second product.
misconception_redirects.say: Draw an arrow from the outside number to each term inside and say the product out loud with its sign: 'negative four times negative seven is positive twenty-eight.' Then combine like terms.
misconception_redirects.praise: You multiplied both terms and kept the signs straight -- clean distribution.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student forgets to multiply the constant by a fractional coefficient (leaves -8 in (1/2)(4x - 8)).
misconception_redirects.say: The 1/2 has to hit the -8 too: half of -8 is -4. Every term inside, no exceptions.
misconception_redirects.praise: You multiplied the constant by the fraction as well -- nothing skipped.

quick_checks.look_for: -3x + 12. An answer of -3x - 12 diagnoses the negative-times-negative sign error.
5x - 5. Leaving -10 unmultiplied means the student skipped the constant.

sentence_starters: The outside number ___ multiplies both ___ and ___.
Negative times negative is positive, so the second product is ___.

steps.annotation: The coefficient multiplies the first inside term.
It must also multiply the constant -- no term skipped.
Now look for like terms.
One x-term and one constant -- simplified.
First product.
Negative times negative is positive.
Write the two products together as one expression.
State the simplified equivalent expression.

skills.name: Factor out the greatest common number to write p(qx + r)
skills.i_do_script: Picture 36x + 9 as one rectangle with height 9, split into two rooms -- one room holds the area 36x, the other holds the area 9, and each room's width is what 9 must multiply to fill it. Factoring is distribution in reverse: I pull the greatest common factor out front and put what is left in parentheses. Watch: 36x + 9. The biggest number that divides both 36 and 9 is 9. I divide each term by 9: 36x divided by 9 is 4x, and 9 divided by 9 is 1. So 36x + 9 = 9(4x + 1). The standard's own example is 2x - 10 = 2(x - 5). I always check by distributing back: 9 times 4x is 36x, 9 times 1 is 9 -- it matches.

canonical_error.pattern: Pulls out a common factor but forgets to divide EVERY term by it (leaves a term unchanged), or uses a factor that isn't the greatest
canonical_error.example: For 36x + 9 the student writes 9(4x + 9), forgetting that 9 divided by 9 = 1, so the second term should be 1, not 9
canonical_error.why: The student divides the first term but copies the second term unchanged, breaking equivalence -- 9(4x + 9) expands to 36x + 81, not 36x + 9. Factoring only works if every term inside is the original term divided by the factor.

skills.item_template: A linear expression ax + b with a common factor; student writes p(qx + r) or p(qx - r) using the greatest common factor. Integer coefficients (a rational factor at the stretch). Multiple choice or short response.

sample_items.distractor_logic: GCF of 36 and 9 is 9: 36x/9 = 4x, 9/9 = 1. '9(4x + 9)'-style errors forget to divide the constant; 36(x + 1) = 36x + 36; 4(9x + 1) = 36x + 4.
GCF is 2: 2x/2 = x, -10/2 = -5. The standard's own example. Forgetting to divide -10 gives 2(x - 10).
GCF (with the negative pulled out) is -12: -72x/-12 = 6x, 60/-12 = -5. Sign errors on the constant give -12(6x + 5).

sample_items.stem: Factor: 15x - 25 using the greatest common factor.
sample_items.distractor_logic: GCF of 15 and 25 is 5: 15x/5 = 3x, -25/5 = -5. Using 3 or another non-greatest factor leaves a further common factor inside.

redirect_script.stop: Divide the constant by the factor too.
redirect_script.prompt: Go back to the rectangle: if the height is 9 and that room's area is only 9, how wide can the room be? After you pull out the factor, divide EACH term by it -- including the constant. Then distribute back to check: it must return the exact original expression.
redirect_script.praise: You divided every term by the factor and checked by distributing -- that's a valid factoring.

vocabulary.definition: A number that divides evenly into every term; to factor is to write the expression as that number times a parenthesis.
The largest number that divides evenly into all the terms, like 9 for 36x and 9.
The rule you use to check a factoring: p(qx + r) = pqx + pr should return the original.

worked_example_script.text: Draw one rectangle cut into two rooms. The left room has area 36x, the right room has area 9. Label the shared height 9 along the side.
With height 9, how wide is the left room -- 9 times what gives 36x? And the right room: 9 times WHAT gives an area of just 9?

The left width is 4x and the right width is 1, because 9 x 1 = 9. Total width 4x + 1, so the whole rectangle is 9(4x + 1). A width of 9 would make that little room's area 81 -- the picture will not allow it.
Write '36x + 9.'
What is the biggest number that divides both 36 and 9?
9 divides both. Divide each term by 9: 36x divided by 9 is 4x, and 9 divided by 9 is 1. So 36x + 9 = 9(4x + 1).
If the student writes 9(4x + 9), ask 'what is 9 divided by 9?'
Check by distributing back, then your turn: factor 2x - 10.

practice_problems.stem: What is the greatest common factor of 12 and 18?

practice_problems.notes: Spec Approaching item; baits forgetting to divide the constant.
The standard's own worked example.

practice_problems.stem: Taylor factored 36x + 9. Find and fix the mistake.
practice_problems.answer: Taylor forgot to divide the constant: 9 divided by 9 = 1, not 9. The correct factoring is 9(4x + 1). Check: 9(4x + 1) = 36x + 9, but 9(4x + 9) = 36x + 81.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: constant left undivided when factoring.
Spec Approaching item; pull out the negative GCF.
Reversed direction -- a non-greatest factor still gives an equivalent form.

practice_problems.stem: Factor 15x - 25 completely, then check by distributing.
practice_problems.notes: Requires the GREATEST factor plus a verification step.

activities.title: Factored or Not
activities.instructions:
1. Each card shows an expression and a proposed factored form.
2. Distribute the factored form back in your head or on paper.
3. Sort the card into 'Correct factoring' or 'Not equivalent.'
4. Rule to place a card: for a wrong one, name which term was not divided.
5. Debrief: which wrong cards forgot to divide the constant?

activities.title: Divide Every Term
activities.instructions:
1. Read Taylor's factoring of 36x + 9 as 9(4x + 9).
2. Distribute 9(4x + 9) back -- what does it actually equal?
3. Redo the division of EACH term by 9 and write the correct factored form.
4. Write a rule: what must you do to every term inside?

content.error_step: Taylor divided 36x by 9 but copied the 9 unchanged.
content.why: 9 divided by 9 is 1, so it is 9(4x + 1). Distributing Taylor's form gives 36x + 81, not 36x + 9 -- proof the constant was not divided.

strategy_links.why: Pairing a correct factoring against the '9(4x + 9)' version makes 'divide every term' explicit through contrast.
The undivided-constant error is a clean, high-frequency factoring mistake for a find-and-fix routine.
An area model (rectangle split into 36x and 9 with side length 9) makes factoring out the common side concrete.

questioning_prompts: What is the greatest number that divides every term?
What is each term divided by that factor?
Did you divide the constant, or copy it?
If you distribute your answer back, do you get the original?
Is there still a common factor left inside the parentheses?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student pulls out a factor but leaves a term undivided, or uses a factor that isn't the greatest.
misconception_redirects.say: After you pull out the factor, divide EACH term by it -- including the constant. Then distribute back to check: it must return the exact original expression.
misconception_redirects.praise: You divided every term by the factor and checked by distributing -- that's a valid factoring.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student factors out a smaller common factor and leaves another one inside (e.g., 2(18x + ...) for 36x).
misconception_redirects.say: Find the GREATEST common factor -- if the parenthesis still shares a factor, pull it out too.
misconception_redirects.praise: You found the greatest factor, so nothing common is left inside -- fully factored.

quick_checks.look_for: 4(5x + 2). '4(5x + 8)' or '2(10x + 4)' diagnose an undivided term or a non-greatest factor.
2(x - 5). '2(x - 10)' means the -10 was not divided by 2.

sentence_starters: The greatest common factor of the terms is ___.
Dividing each term by ___ gives ___, so the factored form is ___.

steps.annotation: Find the largest number dividing every term.
Divide the first term by the factor.
Divide the constant too -- do not copy it.
Distribute back to confirm equivalence.
Largest number dividing both terms.
Divide the first term by 2.
Divide the constant -10 by 2.
Write the factored form and check by distributing.

skills.name: Simplify a multi-step expression and justify each step
skills.i_do_script: Subtracting a group means removing the WHOLE package -- and when the package is a debt, removing it makes you richer. Watch the debt slip get torn up before any rule is spoken. At this level I simplify multi-part expressions using several moves at once and justify each one, which also lets me spot where someone else went wrong. Watch: (2.1x + 4.3) - (-3x - 7). Subtracting a group flips every sign inside: -(-3x - 7) becomes +3x + 7. Now I combine: 2.1x + 3x = 5.1x and 4.3 + 7 = 11.3, so 5.1x + 11.3. The most common slip is in the arithmetic sign -- like doing 2.64 - 4.44 and writing 7.08 (adding) instead of -1.8 (subtracting).

canonical_error.pattern: Adds two constants instead of subtracting when one is negative (a sign slip in the final combine), or forgets that subtracting a group flips every sign inside
canonical_error.example: Simplifying 1.2(2.2 + 3y - 3.7), the student combines the constants 2.64 and -4.44 as 7.08 (adding) instead of -1.8 (subtracting), reporting 7.08 + 3.6y
canonical_error.why: The student ignores the sign of the -4.44 term and adds its absolute value, or drops the sign flip when a whole group is subtracted. Each constant keeps the sign in front of it, and subtracting a group distributes a -1 to every term inside.

skills.item_template: A multi-step simplification (distribute then combine, or subtract a group) shown as student work with one error, OR an expression to simplify with each step justified. Integer and decimal coefficients. DOK 3 multiple choice / short response.

sample_items.stem: A student simplified 1.2(2.2 + 3y - 3.7). Step 1: 1.2(2.2 + 3y - 3.7); Step 2: 2.64 + 3.6y - 4.44; Step 3: 2.64 - 4.44 + 3.6y; Step 4: 7.08 + 3.6y. In which step is the first error?
sample_items.answer: Step 4 -- 2.64 - 4.44 = -1.8, not 7.08 (the student added instead of subtracting).
choices: Step 3 -- the terms cannot be reordered.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Distribution and reordering are correct; the error is adding the constants instead of subtracting. Correct result: 3.6y - 1.8.
Subtracting the group flips signs: +3x + 7. Then 2.1x + 3x = 5.1x, 4.3 + 7 = 11.3. Keeping -3x - 7 gives -0.9x - 2.7.
-3 times -2 = +6, then 6 + 5 = 11. '-3x - 1' comes from making -3 times -2 negative.
3 - 6 = -3 and 2 + 3 = 5. Reading -6x as +6x gives 9x + 5.

redirect_script.stop: Check the sign on that constant before you combine.
redirect_script.prompt: See the group as one package first: what happens to each piece inside when the whole package is taken away? Rewrite each constant with its sign in front, then combine: 2.64 and -4.44 give 2.64 - 4.44 = -1.8. If a whole group is subtracted, flip every sign inside first.
redirect_script.praise: You tracked the sign through the combine -- that's why your justification holds.

vocabulary.definition: A number outside parentheses multiplies each term inside; subtracting a group is multiplying it by -1.
A number plus its opposite is 0; subtracting a term is adding its additive inverse.
A single number or variable piece separated by + or -, each carrying the sign in front of it.

worked_example_script.text: Picture (2.1x + 4.3) as your pile, and (-3x - 7) as a debt slip: 3 bags of x owed and 7 counters owed. Subtracting that group means someone tears up the debt slip.
When a debt of 3 bags and 7 counters disappears, is your pile bigger or smaller? By how many bags, and by how many counters?

Tearing up the debt makes you 3 bags and 7 counters RICHER: subtracting -3x - 7 adds +3x and +7. That is why every sign inside a subtracted group flips -- and why each constant must be combined with the sign it truly carries.
What happens to the signs inside the second group when we subtract it?
Subtracting flips every sign: -(-3x - 7) becomes +3x + 7. Now combine: 2.1x + 3x = 5.1x and 4.3 + 7 = 11.3. Result: 5.1x + 11.3.
If a student keeps -3x - 7, ask 'what does the minus in front of the parenthesis do to each term?'
Your turn: -3(x - 2) + 5. Distribute, then combine -- watch the signs.

practice_problems.stem: When you simplify a(b + c), which comes first: distribute or combine?
practice_problems.answer: Distribute first, then combine like terms.

practice_problems.stem: A student's steps for 1.2(2.2 + 3y - 3.7) are: Step 2: 2.64 + 3.6y - 4.44; Step 3: 2.64 - 4.44 + 3.6y; Step 4: 7.08 + 3.6y. Find and fix the first error.
practice_problems.answer: The first error is in Step 4: the student added 4.44 to 2.64 instead of subtracting. 2.64 - 4.44 = -1.8, so the correct result is 3.6y - 1.8.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error (spec DOK 3 item): sign slip when combining constants.
Spec At item; subtracting a group flips every sign.
Justify each step; negative-times-negative on the constant.
Spec At item; combine with a negative coefficient.

practice_problems.stem: A classmate wrote -3(x - 2) = -3x - 6. Identify and correct the error, and name the rule that fixes it.
practice_problems.answer: -3 times -2 = +6, so -3x + 6. The rule: negative times negative is positive.
practice_problems.notes: Reversed direction -- diagnose then state the rule.

practice_problems.stem: Justify each step: 4(x + 3) becomes 4x + 12 becomes 12 + 4x. Name the property used at each arrow.
practice_problems.answer: First arrow: distributive property; second arrow: commutative property (of addition).
practice_problems.notes: Directly targets 'justify each step' with two different properties.

activities.title: Trace the First Error
materials: Slip with the four-step simplification of 1.2(2.2 + 3y - 3.7)
activities.instructions:
1. Read all four steps of the student's simplification.
2. Check each step in order and find the FIRST one that is wrong -- do not just judge the final answer.
3. Redo from that step forward with the correct sign.
4. Discuss: why does the wrong constant sign not change the y-term but still make the answer wrong?

content.error_step: Step 4: the student added 2.64 + 4.44 = 7.08 instead of subtracting.
content.why: 2.64 - 4.44 = -1.8. The correct simplified expression is 3.6y - 1.8; only the constant was mishandled, but the answer is still wrong.

activities.title: Justify the Step
materials: Card set: 5 step cards and 5 property cards (two decoys)
activities.instructions:
1. Each step card shows one move in a simplification.
2. Match it to the property that justifies that move.
3. Two property cards are decoys -- set them aside and explain why they don't fit.
4. To claim a match, say what changed in the step.
5. Debrief: which step used more than one property?

strategy_links.why: Finding the FIRST wrong step in multi-step work is error analysis at exactly the point the standard's DOK 3 items target.
Thinking aloud 'distribute, then flip the subtracted group, then combine' models the step-by-step justification the standard requires.
Writing the property beside each step turns 'justify each step' into a reflective-writing habit.

questioning_prompts: What is the FIRST step that is wrong -- not just the final answer?
What does the minus in front of a parenthesis do to each term inside?
What property justifies this particular move?
What sign does that constant really carry?
Could you check the whole thing by substituting x = 1?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student adds two constants instead of subtracting, or drops the sign flip on a subtracted group.
misconception_redirects.say: Rewrite each constant with its sign in front, then combine: 2.64 and -4.44 give 2.64 - 4.44 = -1.8. If a whole group is subtracted, flip every sign inside first.
misconception_redirects.praise: You tracked the sign through the combine -- that's why your justification holds.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student judges only the final answer and misses an earlier step error.
misconception_redirects.say: Check the steps in order and stop at the FIRST wrong one -- an early slip carries through everything after it.
misconception_redirects.praise: You found the first error, not just a wrong ending -- that's how you trace a mistake.

quick_checks.look_for: 3x + 5. An answer of 3x - 3 means the student did not flip the signs of the subtracted group.
Distributive. Any other name signals the justification step is not solid.

sentence_starters: First I ___, which is justified by the ___ property.
The sign on that constant is ___, so the combine gives ___.

steps.annotation: Subtracting a group flips every sign inside (distribute -1).
Now all signs are settled -- look for like terms.
Add the coefficients.
One x-term and one constant -- simplified.
Negative times negative is positive.
Bring down the loose 3x.
Combine the x-terms -2x and 3x.
Write the simplified expression.

skills.name: Create and verify multiple equivalent expressions
skills.i_do_script: At the top level I create MULTIPLE equivalent expressions from one, and I can prove two forms are equal. Watch: 6x + 3(2x + 3) + 8x. Distribute the 3: 6x + 6x + 9 + 8x -- that is already one equivalent form, 12x + 9 + 8x. Combine all the x-terms: 6 + 6 + 8 = 20, so the fully simplified form is 20x + 9. To prove two forms match, I substitute a value: at x = 1 the original is 6 + 15 + 8 = 29, and 20x + 9 is 29 -- equal.

canonical_error.pattern: Produces a form that is not actually equivalent -- a sign slip when subtracting a group or a missed term -- instead of a genuinely equal expression
canonical_error.example: For 3x + 5(-4x + 12) - (x - 3) the student writes -x - 3 for the last group (should be -x + 3), reporting -18x + 57 instead of -18x + 63
canonical_error.why: The student treats 'equivalent' as 'looks similar' and skips the substitution check that would catch the error. Two expressions are equivalent only if they give the same value for every input, which a single sign slip destroys.

skills.item_template: A complex expression (distribution plus loose terms, or a subtracted group); student selects ALL equivalent forms or writes two equivalent expressions. Integer coefficients. Multiple select / constructed response.

sample_items.distractor_logic: 3(2x + 3) = 6x + 9. Partially combined: 12x + 9 + 8x; fully: 20x + 9. Distractors use 3(2x+3)=6x+3 (undistributed constant) or wrong sums.
5(-4x + 12) = -20x + 60; -(x - 3) = -x + 3. Fully simplified: -18x + 63. Writing -x - 3 (missed sign flip) gives the non-equivalent -18x + 57.

sample_items.stem: Are 20x + 9 and 12x + 9 + 8x equivalent? Justify with a substitution.
sample_items.answer: Yes -- at x = 1, both equal 29 (12 + 9 + 8 and 20 + 9); combining 12x + 8x gives 20x.
sample_items.distractor_logic: 12x + 8x = 20x, constants match, so equivalent. A substitution check certifies it.

redirect_script.stop: Test both forms with one value before you call them equal.
redirect_script.prompt: Pick x = 1, evaluate the original and your new expression. If they don't match, hunt for a dropped sign -- subtracting a group flips every sign inside, so -(x - 3) is -x + 3.
redirect_script.praise: You verified equivalence by substituting -- that's proof, not a guess.

vocabulary.definition: Expressions that give the same value for every value of the variable, even if they look different.
A number outside parentheses multiplies each term inside: a(b + c) = ab + ac.
A number pulled out of every term; factoring gives another equivalent form, like -12(6x - 5) for -72x + 60.

next_steps.if_pass: Ready for 8.AF.1 (solve linear equations that require expanding and combining) and further algebra.

worked_example_script.text: What is one equivalent form after just distributing the 3?
Distribute: 6x + 6x + 9 + 8x, which is 12x + 9 + 8x -- one equivalent form. Combine all x-terms: 6 + 6 + 8 = 20, giving 20x + 9 -- a second form.
If a student claims a form without checking, say 'substitute x = 1 into both -- do they match?'
Your turn: write two equivalent expressions for 3x + 5(-4x + 12) - (x - 3).

practice_problems.notes: Spec Above item; (b) forgets to distribute the 3 to the constant.
Spec Above item; requires the sign flip on -(x - 3).

practice_problems.stem: Jordan simplified 3x + 5(-4x + 12) - (x - 3) and got -18x + 57. Find and fix the mistake.
practice_problems.answer: Jordan wrote -x - 3 for -(x - 3); subtracting the group flips both signs, so it is -x + 3. The correct simplified form is -18x + 63. Check x = 1: original = 3 + 5(8) - (-2) = 3 + 40 + 2 = 45, and -18(1) + 63 = 45.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: missed sign flip on a subtracted group breaks equivalence.
Spec Approaching item; (b) gives 72x + 60, the wrong sign.

practice_problems.stem: Write -72x + 60 in three different equivalent forms, at least one factored.
practice_problems.notes: Produce multiple forms including a factored one.

practice_problems.stem: Show that 2(x - 5) and 2x - 10 are equivalent, and name the property that connects them.
practice_problems.answer: Distributive property: 2 times x = 2x, 2 times -5 = -10. Check x = 4: 2(4 - 5) = -2 and 2(4) - 10 = -2.
practice_problems.notes: Reversed direction -- prove equivalence and justify with a property.

activities.title: Equivalent Expression Chains
activities.instructions:
1. Draw a start card (like 6x + 3(2x + 3) + 8x).
2. Write three DIFFERENT equivalent forms in the blanks: one after distributing, one partially combined, one fully simplified.
3. Pick x = 2 and evaluate the start card and all three forms -- every value must match.
4. Trade strips; a partner accepts your chain only if all four values are equal.
5. Debrief: how did substitution catch any form that was not really equivalent?

activities.title: Is It Really Equivalent?
activities.instructions:
1. Read Jordan's simplification of 3x + 5(-4x + 12) - (x - 3) ending in -18x + 57.
2. Substitute x = 1 into the original and into -18x + 57 -- do they match?
3. Find the dropped sign and rewrite the correct equivalent form.
4. Write the rule: what does subtracting a group do to every sign inside?

content.why: Subtracting a group flips every sign: -(x - 3) = -x + 3. The correct form is -18x + 63; substituting x = 1 gives 45 for the original but 39 for -18x + 57.

strategy_links.why: Explaining in writing why two forms are equivalent (with a substitution) builds the justification habit the top band demands.
The missed-sign-flip 'equivalent' that isn't equal is a precise, high-value error for a find-and-fix routine flagged by a substitution check.
A whiteboard pass where each student adds one more equivalent form makes generating multiple expressions collaborative and visible.

questioning_prompts: Can you write a second equivalent form that looks different?
How would you PROVE these two forms are equal?
What value did you substitute, and did both forms match?
What does the minus in front of a group do to every term inside?
Which of these look-alike options are actually equivalent, and how do you know?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student offers a 'form' that is not actually equivalent (sign slip on a subtracted group or a missed term).
misconception_redirects.say: Pick x = 1, evaluate the original and your new expression. If they don't match, hunt for a dropped sign -- subtracting a group flips every sign inside, so -(x - 3) is -x + 3.
misconception_redirects.praise: You verified equivalence by substituting -- that's proof, not a guess.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student can produce only the fully simplified form and no other equivalent expression.
misconception_redirects.say: You can stop partway too: after distributing but before combining is still an equivalent form. List the expression at each stage.
misconception_redirects.praise: You saw that an in-progress expression is equivalent too -- that's flexibility with equivalence.

quick_checks.look_for: a and c. Choosing (b) means the student did not distribute 2 to the 3.

quick_checks.prompt: Write one more expression equivalent to 5x + 10.
quick_checks.look_for: Any equal form, e.g., 5(x + 2). A non-equivalent answer signals a distribution or sign error.

sentence_starters: One equivalent form is ___, and a second is ___.
They are equivalent because at x = ___ both equal ___.

steps.annotation: Distributive property expands the parenthesis.
Combine only the first two x-terms -- still equivalent.
Collect all like terms.
Substitution certifies the forms are equal.
The 5 multiplies each inside term.
Subtracting flips every sign inside.
Write all terms together: 3x - 20x + 60 - x + 3.
Combine like terms for the simplified equivalent form.

looking_back.label: Looking Back
looking_back.description: Skills the student should have but may need re-teaching.

diagnostic_flow.description: Start with S3 (distribute a rational coefficient and combine like terms) -- the At-proficiency core of the standard. If they pass, push to S5 (simplify a multi-step expression and justify each step) and S6 (create and verify multiple equivalent expressions). If they fail, split the diagnosis: S1 checks whether they can combine like terms with signs intact, and S2 checks whether they can name the property that justifies a step. S4 (factoring out the greatest common number) branches off as the reverse-of-distribution skill.
